meta.description: Not Aerosmith. Tiny Bradshaw and his orchestra cut it in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951; King Records issued it that December. Aerosmith's version came in 1974.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'The Train Kept A-Rollin''?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aerosmith. Tiny Bradshaw recorded it first, in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951, released by King Records that December. Aerosmith's hard rock version dates from 1974.

answer.label: Not an Aerosmith original — a 1951 Tiny Bradshaw single on King Records
answer.originalArtistDates: 1907-1958 · American jump-blues and R&B bandleader, singer and drummer
answer.sourceLine: Classic-rock radio has played Aerosmith’s version so long that most listeners file the song under Aerosmith, who cut it for “Get Your Wings” in 1974. It was first recorded by bandleader Tiny Bradshaw and his orchestra in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951, and issued by King Records that December as a jump-blues single paired with “Knockin’ Blues.” The composition is credited to Bradshaw with Howie Kay and “Lois Mann” — the latter a pen name used by King’s owner Syd Nathan. Bradshaw’s record never reached the national R&B charts; the song only became famous through a chain of later covers.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: King Records
original.released: Recorded in Cincinnati, Ohio on 6 October 1951 and released by King Records in December 1951 as a two-sided single — on both 10-inch 78 rpm and 7-inch 45 rpm — paired with “Knockin’ Blues.”
original.charted: Did not chart. Despite five other Bradshaw records reaching the R&B top ten for King, this one never appeared on the national R&B charts, though Billboard’s reviewer praised the vocal in its 23 February 1952 issue.
original.writer: Tiny Bradshaw, Lois Mann and Howard Kay
original.cover: Aerosmith recorded their version at the Record Plant in New York in December 1973 and January 1974 and issued it on “Get Your Wings” (Columbia Records, March 1974). The 3:15 single edit released in October 1974 did not chart; the 5:33 album version became the classic-rock standard.

trail: Tiny Bradshaw records it in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951; King Records releases it that December — see the original King 45-4497 single ↗.

Johnny Burnette and the Rock ‘n’ Roll Trio recorded a rockabilly version on 2 July 1956 at Bradley’s Barn in Nashville and Coral released it that September, with Paul Burlison’s deliberately distorted guitar — detailed on Wikipedia ↗.
The Yardbirds record their fuzz-tone arrangement in September 1965 and release it on Epic on 15 November 1965; it becomes the template later bands copy.
Aerosmith release their hard rock version on “Get Your Wings” (Columbia) in March 1974 — the version most listeners now think of as the original.

authors.name: Tiny Bradshaw
authors.heading: Tiny Bradshaw
authors.metaLine: 1907-1958 · American bandleader, singer, pianist and drummer
authors.bio: Myron “Tiny” Bradshaw was born in Youngstown, Ohio in 1907 and led his own swing orchestra from 1934. Signed to Cincinnati’s King Records, he placed five records on the Billboard R&B chart between late 1949 and early 1955, including the number-two hit “Well Oh Well.” His band was a finishing school for players such as tenor saxophonist Red Prysock, who blows on the 1951 session. A stroke in 1954 curtailed his career, and he died in Cincinnati in 1958 at fifty-one, long before the song he cut became a rock standard.

authors.name: Aerosmith
authors.heading: Aerosmith
authors.metaLine: Formed 1970 in Boston · American hard rock band
authors.bio: Aerosmith recorded the song at the Record Plant in New York between December 1973 and January 1974 and released it on their second album, “Get Your Wings,” on Columbia in March 1974. Their arrangement is in two distinct parts — a slow, groove-heavy opening that erupts into a full-tilt rocker — with lead guitar contributions from session players Steve Hunter and Dick Wagner. An edited single followed in October 1974 and did not chart, but the album version became a fixture of album-oriented rock radio and remains one of the band’s best-known performances. The record is superb; only the assumption that they wrote or first cut it is wrong.

authors.name: Tiny Bradshaw, Howie Kay and Lois Mann
authors.heading: The credited writers
authors.metaLine: Credited on the 1951 King Records single and in the MusicBrainz work entry
authors.bio: The composition is registered to three names: Tiny Bradshaw, Howie Kay and Lois Mann. Bradshaw built the song by reworking the earlier “Cow-Cow Boogie” (1942) into an urban, hipster train scenario. “Lois Mann” was a pen name used by King Records owner Syd Nathan, a common label-owner device for taking a cut of publishing income; historian Larry Birnbaum has written that Kay’s identity remains obscure. The original King 45 label itself carried only a Bradshaw–Mann credit.

misattribution.heading: Setting the record straight
misattribution.intro: Aerosmith’s 1974 recording is the one most people have heard, and for many listeners it is simply where the song comes from. The paperwork says otherwise.

items.why: Their two-part hard rock version appeared on “Get Your Wings” (Columbia) in March 1974 and became a classic-rock staple. The October 1974 single edit did not chart. They were working from the Yardbirds’ 1965 arrangement, not from scratch.

Recorded in Cincinnati on 6 October 1951 and released by King Records that December on 78 and 45 (catalogue 45-4497), paired with “Knockin’ Blues.” A jump-blues record with horns and shuffle rhythm. It did not appear on the national R&B charts.

items.who: Tiny Bradshaw, Howie Kay and Lois Mann
items.why: “Lois Mann” was a pen name used by King Records owner Syd Nathan — a label-boss share of the publishing rather than a contribution to the song. Bradshaw derived the piece from the earlier “Cow-Cow Boogie” (1942).

items.who: Johnny Burnette’s Rock ‘n’ Roll Trio and The Yardbirds
items.why: Burnette’s Coral single of September 1956 carried Paul Burlison’s distorted guitar; the Yardbirds’ Epic release of November 1965 set the fuzz-tone arrangement that Aerosmith and everyone after them followed.

misattribution.truthLine: First recorded by Tiny Bradshaw, 6 October 1951, released by King Records in December 1951. Aerosmith’s version is the fourth well-known one.

context.heading: How a jump-blues B-list single became an Aerosmith song
lead: The song did not travel from Bradshaw to Aerosmith in one leap — it was handed along. Johnny Burnette and the Rock ‘n’ Roll Trio recorded it on 2 July 1956 in Nashville and Coral released it that September, and guitarist Paul Burlison’s deliberately distorted tone on that record is often cited as one of the first intentional uses of guitar distortion on a rock recording. The Yardbirds cut their version in September 1965 and released it that November on Epic; Jeff Beck’s fuzz-tone arrangement became the template everyone afterwards followed, and Led Zeppelin later used it as a concert opener.

By the time Aerosmith reached it in 1974, the song had been a rock song for eighteen years and a jump-blues record for less than five. The scale of that eclipse is captured by a remark Jeff Beck reported hearing from listeners — that they liked his angle on the Aerosmith tune. If the man whose arrangement Aerosmith were working from got mistaken for the imitator, a 1951 Cincinnati bandleader never stood a chance.
context.detailsSummary: The chain of custody, step by step
detailsBody: 6 October 1951 — Tiny Bradshaw and his orchestra record the song in Cincinnati, Ohio.
December 1951 — King Records issues it on 10-inch 78 and 7-inch 45 (catalogue 45-4497), paired with “Knockin’ Blues.” The record does not reach the national R&B charts.
23 February 1952 — Billboard’s Rhythm & Blues Record Reviews column praises the vocal on what it calls a rocking novelty.
September 1956 — Johnny Burnette and the Rock ‘n’ Roll Trio release a rockabilly version on Coral, with Paul Burlison’s distorted guitar.
September–November 1965 — The Yardbirds record and release their fuzz-tone arrangement on Epic; it becomes the version later bands copy.
March 1974 — Aerosmith release their two-part hard rock version on “Get Your Wings” (Columbia). A single edit follows in October 1974 and does not chart.
context.pull: Bradshaw’s record never charted. Neither did anyone else’s — the song outlived the charts entirely.
